newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela's president vows to continue reforms.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela's president vows to continue reforms.

text.p: Venezuelan President Rafael Caldera vowed in his traditional end-of-the-year message to continue tough economic reforms but gave thanks that, despite a hard year, Venezuela was still a country at peace.
"If we don't keep a firm hand, we'll loose the ground gained, and everyone must understand this," Caldera, 80, said in a live television broadcast.

Venezuela -- which closed the year with the region's highest inflation rate, and also the world's fastest growing stock market -- implemented a tough series of economic reforms supported by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in April.
When similar reforms were tried in 1992, riots rocked the capital leaving some 300 dead.
"We have to give thanks to God that we have peace in Venezuela. This peace we must conserve and further because its our strongest weapon for the future," said Caldera, who rarely speaks in public.
The reform package, called Venezuelan Agenda, included price hikes, tax increases and the freeing of exchange and interest rate controls.
"It has been on balance a very positive year ... although with negative aspects," Caldera said.

But if Venezuela did not continue the reforms, "the hydra-headed monster of inflation, of which we've chopped off a head, could come back," he added. Inflation, which peaked at more than 12 percent monthly in May and has since fallen to just over two, closed the year at an annual rate of 103 percent.
"Everyone now recognises the will of the Venezuelan government and people to continue the measures introduced in April," he said.

Caldera, who was elected president for the second time in February 1994 under promises to never go to the IMF, said 1997 would see the government target social spending even as it kept a firm lid on spending. An estimated eight out of 10 Venezuelans now live in poverty.
"God gives victory to the constant," he closed, quoting the 19th century hero of South American independence Simon Bolivar.
